title: 1 Samuel 8:1–9
context: Samuel has grown old, and the sons he appoints as judges in Beersheba pervert justice for gain. The elders of Israel come to him at Ramah and ask for a king to judge them like all the nations. Samuel is displeased and prays, and the LORD tells him to listen to the people, because they have rejected not Samuel but the LORD himself as king, just as they have forsaken him since the exodus. Samuel is to grant the request while solemnly warning them about the way of the king. Both traditions share the main reading: the request is sinful in its motive, God remains Israel’s true King, and he still governs the outcome while holding the people responsible.

verses.text: When Samuel was old, he made his sons judges over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the chapter opens with a human decision: Samuel, now old, makes his sons judges. No divine word is recorded for the appointment, and the story that follows shows how genuine human choices, even by a faithful leader, open real paths with real consequences for the whole nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records Samuel’s act without comment, yet the scene begins the turn toward kingship that the books of Samuel trace to David. Even an unwise human arrangement is taken up within God’s ordering of Israel’s history, without making the arrangement itself good or wise.

verses.text: Now the name of his firstborn was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the naming of Joel and Abijah as a sober reminder that faith is not passed down automatically. Each generation must answer God for itself, and the sons of a godly father can choose a different path, much as Eli’s sons did earlier in the book (1 Samuel 2:12–17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the painful echo of Eli’s house (1 Samuel 2:12–17). Covenant privilege does not guarantee covenant faithfulness, and grace does not run in bloodlines; the LORD keeps his promises to Israel even when the households of its leaders fail to walk in his ways.

verses.text: His sons didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers stress that the sons’ corruption is described as their own turning: they turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice. The law already forbade such conduct (Deuteronomy 16:19), so they are fully accountable for misusing the office entrusted to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the sons are fully culpable and note that their bribery breaks the law’s plain command (Deuteronomy 16:19). Their failure exposes the limits of every human judge and prepares readers to long for a ruler who will judge with true righteousness, a hope the Scriptures later fix on David’s line.

verses.text: Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together and came to Samuel to Ramah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the elders act through recognized channels, gathering together and coming to Samuel at Ramah, his home (1 Samuel 7:17). Their concern about corrupt judges is real, and the narrative takes their grievance seriously even as it will question the remedy they choose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the elders’ approach is orderly and their complaint has substance. The problem the chapter exposes lies not in seeking better leadership as such but in the heart behind the request, which the LORD himself will soon reveal to Samuel in his answer.

verses.text: They said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the phrase “like all the nations” as the heart of the problem. Israel had been called to be distinct, and the elders choose to measure security by the pattern of their neighbors rather than by trust in the LORD who had just delivered them at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:10–13).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a king was anticipated in the law (Deuteronomy 17:14–20) and in the promises to the patriarchs, so kingship itself is not the sin. The fault lies in the motive of wanting to be “like all the nations,” seeking a visible substitute for the invisible King who had saved them.

verses.text: But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commend Samuel’s response: displeased, he does not lash out or simply refuse, but prays to the LORD. A leader’s first recourse in a crisis is honest prayer, and the narrative presents God as one who hears and answers such prayer in a real exchange with his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise highlight that Samuel takes the matter to the LORD before acting. His displeasure is understandable, yet he submits the question to God’s word, modeling dependence on divine direction rather than on personal hurt or on the pressure of the people’s demand.

verses.text: The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that God tells Samuel to listen to the people even though their request is a rejection of the LORD himself. God permits a choice he does not approve, honoring the real agency he has given his people while naming the request for what it is and holding them accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the people truly reject the LORD and that God names it plainly. They add that God’s instruction to grant the request shows his sovereignty over even sinful human desire: he directs the outcome toward his own ends, including a later king after his own heart, without approving the people’s motive.

verses.text: According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, in that they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they also do to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD tracing a long pattern: from the exodus onward the people have forsaken him and served other gods. Their present request is one more free act in a history of repeated unfaithfulness, and God’s grief over it is presented as real and relational.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD interprets the request in light of Israel’s whole history of idolatry since the exodus. The sin is not new but expresses a persistent bent of the heart away from God, which underscores how deeply Israel needs grace that only God can supply.

verses.text: Now therefore, listen to their voice. However, you shall protest solemnly to them, and shall show them the way of the king who will reign over them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers stress that God grants the request only with a solemn warning. He respects the people’s choice but makes sure they choose with open eyes, showing them the way of the king, so that the consequences that follow are the fruit of a decision they were clearly warned about.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a gracious warning attached to God’s permission. The LORD gives the people what they ask while testifying against them, so that his justice is clear and his purposes for kingship move forward; both traditions see real divine patience in this instruction to Samuel.
